summary: Defines how to use the Lempel-Ziv-Stac (LZS) compression algorithm inside the TLS protocol. TLS lets two sides negotiate lossless compression, but its only standard method at the time was no compression at all.

plainLanguage.summary: TLS can secure a connection and can also agree to squeeze the data before sending it. This memo defines one way to do the squeezing, so that long connections over a secure tunnel need less bandwidth.

questions: how to compress data in tls
what is the tls compression method number for lzs
subtitle: How to squeeze TLS record payloads with the Lempel-Ziv-Stac algorithm, using compression method number 64.

tldr.problem: TLS can negotiate a compression method, but its only standard one was null, which means no compression. That left no interoperable way to save bandwidth on long-lived or high-volume TLS connections such as VPNs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an LZS compression method for TLS. Each record gets a one-octet header with a reset bit and a compressed/uncompressed bit, and the compressor keeps a 2,048-byte history across the records of one session.
tldr.outcome: LZS gets compression method identifier 64 from IANA. The RFC warns that compressing before encrypting can leak information through message length, and that the history holds plaintext. It has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3943 is an Informational RFC from November 2004. It provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and it has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Why TLS Needed a Compression Method
sections.content:
The Transport Layer Security protocol includes features to negotiate a lossless data compression method as part of the TLS Handshake Protocol, and then to apply the chosen algorithm as part of the TLS Record Protocol. TLS defines one standard compression method, CompressionMethod.null, which specifies that data exchanged via the record protocol will not be compressed. The RFC notes that this single method helps ensure that TLS implementations interoperate, but that the lack of additional standard compression methods has limited the ability to develop interoperable implementations that include data compression.

TLS secures a great many short client-server connections on the World Wide Web, but it is also used where connections can be long-lived and the data exchanged can extend into thousands or millions of octets. TLS is now increasingly used as an alternative Virtual Private Network connection, and compression services have long been associated with IPSec and PPTP VPN connections, so extending compression to TLS VPN connections preserves the user experience for any VPN connection. Compression inside TLS is one way to reduce the bandwidth and latency requirements of exchanging large amounts of data while keeping the security services TLS provides.

This document describes an additional compression method, based on the Lempel-Ziv-Stac (LZS) lossless data compression algorithm, and defines the application of the LZS algorithm to TLS record payloads. It assumes a thorough understanding of the TLS protocol in RFC 2246.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS can agree to compress the data it carries, but the only standard method was to do nothing, so no two implementations could both compress and still interoperate. This memo defines one that can.

sections.title: The LZS Compression Method
sections.content:
The LZS CompressionMethod is a 16-bit index, negotiated as described in RFC 2246 and RFC 3749, and stored in the TLS Record Layer connection state. IANA has assigned 64 as the compression method identifier for applying LZS compression to TLS record payloads, and section 6 records that identifier as 64 decimal, which is 0x40, taken from the RFC 2434 Specification Required IANA pool described in RFC 3749.

Compression methods used with TLS can be stateful, where the compressor keeps its state through all compressed records, or stateless, where each record is compressed on its own. The RFC says there seems to be little known benefit in using a stateless method within TLS, and the LZS method it defines is stateful. Stateful compression gives a higher compression ratio than stateless compression, particularly for small records, and it needs a reliable link and sequenced record delivery so that all records can be decompressed in the order they were compressed. TLS and the protocols below it provide that, so the compression history may be maintained and exploited.

The LZS algorithm itself uses a sliding window of 2,048 bytes. During compression, redundant sequences of data are replaced with tokens that represent those sequences, and during decompression the original sequences are put back in place of the tokens so that the original data is recovered exactly. LZS is lossless, unlike the lossy algorithms often used for video, and it provides compression for strings as short as two octets in length. The worst-case expansion factor of LZS is only 12.5%, so TLS records of 15K bytes can never exceed the expansion limits of section 6.2.2 of RFC 2246.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides agree on a number, 64, that means we squeeze our data with LZS. They also both remember the last part of what they sent, which helps squeeze the next record even more.

sections.title: The One-Octet TLSComp Header
sections.content:
Before compression, the uncompressed data, the TLSPlaintext fragment, is a plaintext TLS record. After compression, the compressed data, the TLSCompressed fragment, is an 8-bit TLSComp header followed by the compressed or uncompressed data. The header is a single Flags octet with three parts.

Res is six reserved bits. They MUST be set to zero and MUST be ignored by the receiving node. RST tells the decompressing peer that the compression history in this session was reset before the data in this record was compressed; when it is 1 a history reset is performed, and when it is 0 it is not. This bit MUST be set to 1 for the first compressed record transmitted in a session, and it may also be used by the transmitter for other exception cases where the history has to be reset. C/U says whether the data field holds compressed or uncompressed data: a value of 1 means compressed, and 0 means uncompressed.

The compressed payload is encoded as defined in ANSI X3.241, and the RFC repeats that encoding for information only, noting that it is also described in RFC 1967, RFC 1974 and RFC 2395. A compressed payload always ends with an end marker, which is used to disambiguate padding, so trailing bits as well as trailing bytes can be treated as padding, and the size of a compressed payload MUST be in whole octet units.
sections.plainLanguage: Each compressed record starts with one octet of flags. One bit says the compression history was reset before this record, and one bit says whether the record holds compressed or uncompressed data. The other six bits are reserved and must be zero.

sections.title: The LZS Encoding Format
sections.content:
The encoding format describes each compressed record as a series of compressed strings followed by an end marker. A compressed string is either a raw byte or a pair of offset and length, where the offset points back into the compression history and the length says how many bytes to copy from there. The offset is a 7-bit value when its leading bit is 1 and an 11-bit value when it is 0, and the length is coded in a variable-width form that reaches 24 bytes.

The end marker is the bit pattern 110000000. A datagram payload compressed with LZS always ends with the last compressed data byte, which is that end marker, and that is what lets trailing bits and bytes be treated as padding.
sections.plainLanguage: Each squeezed record is a list of short items. Some are literal bytes. Others say how many bytes to copy from earlier in the same record's history. A special bit pattern marks the end.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Records
sections.content:
On the sending side, a TLS record is assigned to a TLS context that includes the LZS compression history buffer, and it is processed according to ANSI X3.241-1994 to form compressed data, or used as is to form uncompressed data. The compression history MUST be cleared for the first record of the session and for exception conditions, and it MUST be updated whenever either a compressed or an uncompressed record is produced. The sender MUST flush the compressor each time it transmits a compressed record, which means that all data going into the compressor is included in the output, so no data is retained in the hope of better compression; flushing prevents a record's data from spilling over into a later record and keeps the compressed data in step with the authenticated and encrypted data in the TLS record.

On the receiving side, the receiver MUST reset the decompression history before decompressing the first compressed record of the session, and subsequent records are decompressed in the order received. After a record is received from the peer and decrypted, the RST and C/U bits MUST be checked. If C/U is 1 the data MUST be decompressed. If C/U is 0 the decompression history MUST be updated with the received uncompressed data. If RST is 1 the receiving decompression history MAY be reset to an initial state before decompressing the record, although due to the characteristics of the Hifn LZS algorithm such a reset is not required.

Two workable options exist for records that expand. The first is to send the expanded data, as long as the TLSCompressed length stays at 17K or less, and maintain the history, which loses current bandwidth but preserves future bandwidth. The second is to send the uncompressed data and not clear the compression history, so the decompressor updates its own history, which conserves both current and future bandwidth; the RFC says this second option is the preferred one and SHOULD be implemented. A third option, sending the uncompressed data and clearing the history, SHOULD NOT be implemented, since it may lose future compression on the link.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a compression history for the whole session and flushes the compressor at the end of every record, so no data carries over into the next one. The receiver resets its history before the first record, then follows the two flag bits to decide what to do with each record.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the document introduces no topics that alter the threat model addressed by TLS, so the security considerations described throughout RFC 2246 apply here as well. It then warns about one thing that compression adds: combining compression with encryption can reveal information that would not have been revealed without it. Data that is the same length before compression might be a different length afterwards, so an adversary that observes the length of the compressed data might be able to derive information about the corresponding uncompressed data. Some symmetric encryption ciphersuites do not hide the length of symmetrically encrypted data at all, and others hide it only to some extent: ciphersuites that use stream cipher encryption without padding do not hide length at all, while ciphersuites that use Cipher Block Chaining encryption with padding provide some length hiding, depending on how the amount of padding is chosen. Use of TLS compression SHOULD take into account that the length of compressed data may leak more information than the length of the original uncompressed data.

The second issue is that the LZS compression history contains plaintext, specifically the last 2K bytes of plaintext of the session. Implementations MUST use separate compression histories for each TLS session, because pathological compressed data can potentially reference data prior to the beginning of the current record and a shared history might leak information between sessions. When the session terminates, the implementation SHOULD treat the history as it does any plaintext, for example by freeing the memory and overwriting its contents, the same way it handles TLS key material.
sections.plainLanguage: Compressing before encrypting can leak information through the length of the data, because the same input can compress to different lengths. The compression history also holds the last 2K bytes of plaintext, and it should be cleared away when the session ends.

fields.name: Res
fields.desc: Six reserved bits. MUST be set to zero and MUST be ignored by the receiving node.

fields.name: RST
fields.desc: 1 means the compression history was reset before this record was compressed.

fields.name: C/U
fields.desc: 1 means compressed data, 0 means uncompressed data.

viz.caption: THE LZS ENCODING, REPEATED FROM RFC 3943

data.title: LZS compressed stream
data.code:
<Compressed Stream> := [<Compressed String>*] <End Marker>
<Compressed String> := 0 <Raw Byte> | 1 <Compressed Bytes>

<Raw Byte> := <b><b><b><b><b><b><b><b>          (8-bit byte)
<Compressed Bytes> := <Offset> <Length>

<Offset> := 1 <b><b><b><b><b><b><b> |           (7-bit offset)
           0 <b><b><b><b><b><b><b><b><b><b> (11-bit offset)
<End Marker> := 110000000
<b> := 1 | 0
